desc:
Convert the non-negative integer num to its English words. To keep the answer a single token, write every word with a capital first letter and join the words with no separators (no spaces, no hyphens, no "And").

Use the words One to Nineteen, Twenty, Thirty, Forty, Fifty, Sixty, Seventy, Eighty, Ninety, and the scale words Hundred, Thousand, Million, Billion. Zero is "Zero". A scale word is written only if its group is non-zero, so 1,000,010 is "OneMillionTen".

Examples: 123 gives "OneHundredTwentyThree"; 12345 gives "TwelveThousandThreeHundredFortyFive"; 1000000 gives "OneMillion".
hints: Split the number into groups of three digits: billions, millions, thousands and the last three digits. Each group is written like a number below 1000 followed by its scale word.
Write a helper for numbers 1..999: hundreds digit plus Hundred, then the remaining two digits. Numbers below 20 have their own words; for 20..99 use a tens word and then the ones digit.
Skip groups that are zero (otherwise you would print things like ZeroThousand), handle num == 0 separately, and concatenate the pieces from the largest group to the smallest.
editorial: Every number below 231 has at most four groups of three digits. Process the groups from the largest scale (109) to 1, using q = num // scale and num %= scale. When q is non-zero, append the words for q followed by the scale word.

The words for a group q in 1..999 are built from lookup tables: if q ≥ 100 add ones[q // 100] + "Hundred" and reduce q %= 100; if q ≥ 20 add tens[q // 10] and reduce q %= 10; finally add ones[q] (where ones[0] is the empty string and the table continues through Nineteen). The hard part is not the algorithm but the details: the teens, zero groups in the middle (1,000,010), and the special case 0. Time is constant.
